schools.summary: Matthew Henry reads Manasseh's accession as the same record as 2 Kings 21 and the tragedy of a godly father's son who unravelled Hezekiah's reformation; parents may give good things but not grace.
Gill notes the account is nearly word for word with 2 Kings 21 and refers the reader there.
Clarke surveys the whole reign and presses the riddle: a boy with a pious education, how could its principles be so soon eradicated?
Keil and Delitzsch set the verdict at the head of the catalogue of sins and mark the damning measure — the abominations of the heathen God cast out before Israel, a moral undoing of the conquest.
Gill glosses the 'evil' as idolatry, the same in substance as 2 Kings 21.
Henry reads the verse as the unravelling of Hezekiah's reformation and a warning that corruptions in worship are diseases the church readily relapses into.
Ellicott reads 'the Baals' and 'Asheras' as rhetorical plurals (Kings has singulars, and adds 'as Ahab made'); Keil sets the whole apostasy in ordered sequence.
Clarke identifies the Baalim as sun and moon, the groves as Asheroth/Astarte, and the host of heaven as the planets and stars.
Henry reads the rebuilding of Hezekiah's ruined high places as the deliberate unravelling of his father's reformation.

Ellicott marks that Manasseh built temple altars as Ahaz had done (2 Kings 16:10) and that the chronicler heightens Kings' 'I will set my name' to 'shall my name be for ever'; Keil lets the enormity stand.
Gill reads it as one more stroke of the idolatry recorded in 2 Kings 21.
Henry names the act a profaning of the house of God with idolatry.
Keil marks that altars for the host of heaven were built in both courts of the temple — priests' court and great court alike — so that no part of the sacred precinct was left undefiled.
Clarke identifies the host of heaven as the planets and stars and refers the astral cult to the fuller notes on 2 Kings 21.
Henry reads it as the profaning of God's chosen temple and the debauching of his chosen people.

themes: host of heaven in both courts
the creature adored before the Creator

schools.summary: Ellicott unfolds each forbidden art — augury ('observing clouds'), divination ('observing serpents'), muttered spells, necromancy — traces them to Babylon (cf. Lev. 19:26), and sets Manasseh's turn to darkness against the Assyrian terror described by Robertson Smith.
Henry compresses it: Manasseh dedicated his children to Moloch and made the devil's lying oracles his guides and counsellors.

Ellicott reads the 'carven image of the idol' (semel) as the Asherah of Kings, the words echoing the law's prohibition in Deuteronomy 4:16, set in the Temple proper claimed by God 'for ever'; Keil marks it the summit of the defilement.
Clarke, with the Targum, takes the image to be a likeness of Manasseh himself, set up that he might procure divine honours.

debates.question: What was the 'carved image' Manasseh set in the house of God?

sides.position: a likeness of Manasseh himself, seeking divine honours
the image of Asherah, the idol he had made

themes: a graven image in the holy place

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the promise as frankly conditional ('if only' they take heed), notes the chronicler's changes from Kings, and stresses that 'by the hand of Moses' marks the Lawgiver's authority as God's own, only derived through Moses.
Henry reads the verse as the covenant Manasseh held in contempt — Zion chosen as God's rest for ever and Israel as his covenant-people.

themes: the conditional promise of the land
the law by the hand of Moses

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'led Judah astray, to do evil more than the nations,' and reports Thenius's conjecture that the clause once followed directly on the setting of the graven image.
Henry presses the logic of relapse — worse than the heathen because privileged above them; the unclean spirit returns with seven more wicked than himself.
Gill takes the seduction of Judah as the summary of the apostasy recorded in 2 Kings 21.

outliers.note: Reports Thenius's source-critical view that 'and Manasseh led astray' once stood immediately after 'he set the graven image,' the intervening words being an editor's addition in Kings.

themes: a king who makes a people to sin

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the prophetic sentence from 2 Kings 21:10-15 and the shedding of innocent blood that filled Jerusalem, reading a bloody suppression of the reform party; Keil draws the causal line from the refused word to the Assyrian invasion.
Gill notes God spoke by his servants the prophets.
Henry weighs the grace of God's speaking against the obstinacy of the deaf ear — his goodness waiting, their badness hating to be reformed.

themes: the deaf ear that summons judgment

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott render 'among the thorns' as 'with hooks' (cf. Job 41:2; 2 Kings 19:28), the captured king figured as a ringed beast; Ellicott weighs Esarhaddon against Assurbanipal, cites the tribute inscriptions, and allows a place-name 'Hohim.'
Gill names Esarhaddon and dates the captivity to Manasseh's twenty-second year.
Wesley explains 'king of Assyria' of the Babylonian who had annexed Assyria, and traces the invasion to the treasures the ambassadors had seen.
Henry reads 'among the thorns' figuratively — Manasseh perplexed and 'in the briers,' bound with iron who was held with the cords of his own iniquity.

debates.question: What is meant by 'took Manasseh among the thorns'?

sides.position: with hooks, as a beast ringed through the nose
figuratively, perplexed and ensnared 'in the briers'

debates.question: Which Assyrian king carried Manasseh away?

sides.position: Esarhaddon or rather Assurbanipal, to both of whom he paid tribute

schools.summary: Keil marks the humbling as the reverse of Ahaz's response to the same affliction (2 Chron. 28:22) and notes the genuine prayer is lost; Ellicott glosses 'besought' as 'stroked the face' (Exod. 32:11) and hears pathos in 'the God of his fathers' whom he had forsaken.
Clarke relays the Chaldee legend of the brazen mule and the failed appeal to his idols; Wesley draws the lesson that sinners must humble themselves before the God they have offended.
Gill sets the scene in prison and fetters and preserves the tradition of the pierced brazen instrument.

outliers.note: Relays the Chaldee tradition of a brazen mule bored with holes and heated with fire, in which Manasseh vainly sought his idols before repenting.

themes: humbling before the God of his fathers

schools.summary: Keil notes the restoration to the kingdom; Ellicott sets it beside the parallel restoration of the Egyptian king Necho by Assurbanipal and compares 'the LORD he was God' with 1 Kings 18:39.
Henry reads God's readiness to welcome the returning sinner — afflictions last only till their work is done — and makes Manasseh a pattern of long-suffering (1 Tim. 1:16).
Gill reads the prayer as a cry for mercy and forgiveness, granted.
Clarke relays the Targum's legend of the shut gates of heaven and the window under the throne, calling it childish yet holding that the rabbins hid deep meanings in it.

outliers.note: Relays the Targum legend of angels shutting the gates of prayer and God opening a window under his throne, the prison bursting and the Spirit from the cherubim restoring the king.

themes: prayer heard and the kingdom restored
Manasseh knew the LORD was God

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the wall's exact course — completing Hezekiah's outer wall (2 Chron. 32:5), by the fish gate, round Ophel — and finds its circumstantial detail almost compels a real historical source; Keil weighs whether it is identical with Hezekiah's wall.
Gill takes it for a wall broken by the Assyrian army, identified with Vitringa as the old wall by the pool of Siloah.
Clarke reads it as a weak place or breach the Assyrians had made, now rebuilt.
Henry makes the wall a parable — by sin he had unwalled the city; returning to God in duty, God returned to him in mercy and he rebuilt it.

Keil specifies the clearing of the idols from the two courts and the casting of the altars out of the city; Ellicott fixes the terms (elohe nekar, the Asherah) but notes the reform was incomplete, some altars remaining for Josiah (2 Kings 23:12).
Clarke reads the purge as proof of a real conversion — Manasseh did all he could to destroy his idolatry and restore true worship, bringing forth fruits meet for repentance.
Gill notes the removal of the strange gods and the idol from the house of the LORD.
Henry marks the inward turn — the king now loathes the idols he once loved, and casts them out of the city.

themes: an incomplete reform left for Josiah

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott weigh the variant 'built'/'prepared,' preferring the milder 'prepared'; Ellicott reports Ewald's inference from 'built' that Manasseh had torn down the altar of burnt offering and even destroyed the ark (Jer. 3:16).
Gill takes the altar as fallen to ruin through disuse, or by the margin as one Manasseh 'built' after pulling it down.
Henry reads the repaired altar, the peace and thank offerings, and the command to Judah as a repentance that labours to recover those it once misled — making the plaster as wide as the wound.

debates.question: Does 'built the altar' mean Manasseh had earlier demolished it?

sides.position: he merely repaired/'prepared' a long-neglected altar; its removal would have been noted
he had torn down the altar of burnt offering (and even destroyed the ark), so 'built' is literal

outliers.note: Reports Ewald's conjecture that Manasseh destroyed the ark of the covenant, inferred from the silence of Jeremiah 3:16.

schools.summary: Clarke confirms from the Targum that the high-place worship was now to the Word of the LORD only; Wesley draws the lesson that Manasseh could not carry the reformation as far as he had carried the corruption.
Gill fixes the limit — the people sacrificed still in the high places, but to the LORD and not to idols.
Keil lets the half-reform stand: the high places tolerated, but the worship now rendered to the LORD alone, short of the law's central sanctuary.
Henry notes Manasseh brought the people off their false gods but not their high places — the deeper the corruption, the harder to uproot.

Ellicott identifies the words of the seers, incorporated in the great history of the kings, as a principal source (2 Kings 21:17 pointing to the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah); Keil distinguishes the history of the kings from the sayings of the seer.
Wesley explains 'the book of the kings of Israel' as the public records of Judah (often called Israel), not the canonical book of Kings.
Gill takes the notice to cover all Manasseh's acts, good and bad, before and after his conversion.
Henry marks the prominence given to the prayer, twice mentioned, written for later generations to praise God's readiness to receive returning prodigals.

themes: the prayer honoured on the record

schools.summary: Ellicott argues 'Hozai' is a mutilated form of ha-hozim, 'the seers,' and notes the chronicler heightens Kings' 'his sin' to 'all his sin and unfaithfulness'; Keil summarizes the recorded contents.
Clarke reports the versions' readings of the name — Chozai (Targum, Vulgate), Hunan (Syriac), Saphan (Arabic) — as a proper name.
Gill notes the prayer was recorded in the writings of another, named afterward.
Henry reads the listing of the sins 'before he was humbled' as drawn from the king's own penitent confession, taking shame to himself.

debates.question: Is 'Hozai' a proper name or a corruption of 'the seers'?

sides.position: a proper name — Chozai, or Hunan, or Saphan, as the versions render
a mutilated form of ha-hozim, 'the seers'

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil supply from Kings the fuller 'garden of his house, the garden of Uzza,' the words 'in the garden of' having dropped from the chronicler's text; the burial was not in the royal sepulchres.
Gill explains 'in his own house' of the garden, and notes the ancient custom of burying the dead within the dwelling, whence the household gods.
Henry reads the private, less-honoured burial as a lesson: penitents may recover their comfort sooner than their credit.

themes: buried in the garden of his house

schools.summary: Keil finds the two records agree but for the chronicler's omission of the mother's name, the briefer account, and the added remark that Amon did not humble himself; Ellicott confirms the age against 2 Kings 21:19.
Clarke marks the two-year reign and refers to the fuller notes on 2 Kings 21.
Henry sets the key: little is recorded of Amon, but enough, unless it were better.

themes: an example set to be squandered

schools.summary: Keil summarizes the reproduced idolatry; Ellicott notes the images were cast aside rather than destroyed, but guards Manasseh's reform against Reuss — the words need not mean the very same images.
Henry answers those who doubt Manasseh's repentance (good men have had wicked sons), but faults the reform for not burning the images as Deuteronomy 7:2 required, leaving them for Amon to find.
Clarke voices the astonishment — with his father's example before him, Amon copied the vices but not the repentance.

themes: the son copies the father's sin
the law's demand to burn the images

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the verse as the chronicler's own addition and renders 'for he, Amon, multiplied trespass'; Keil sets the bare contrast — Manasseh humbled himself, Amon did not but increased his guilt.
Henry draws the doctrine: it is not so much sin as impenitence that ruins men — Amon fell like his father but did not get up again; and warns against presuming to repent later.
Clarke reads Amon as exceeding his father and taking no warning.

themes: the folly of presuming to repent later

schools.summary: Henry reads the assassination as fit retribution — 'he rebelled against God, and his own servants rebelled against him' — a young king cut off in impenitence, God righteous though the conspirators wicked.
Clarke owns that the reason for the servants' conspiracy is unknown.
Keil sets down the bare fact of the conspiracy and the killing in the king's own house.
Henry vindicates the execution of the conspirators as traitors, the lives of kings being under the protection of Providence and the laws of God and man.
Clarke reads the mixed motives — the murder was unpopular, yet the avenging people were themselves as prone to idolatry as their king.
Keil records the conspirators slain and Josiah made king in Amon's stead.

themes: a reformer preserved out of apostasy
